etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English request, from Old French requeste (French requête), from Vulgar Latin *requaesita, from Latin requīsīta, feminine of requīsītus (“requested, demanded”), past participle of requīrō (“require, ask”), composed of re- + quaerō (“I seek, look for”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”). Compare to French requérir.

definitions.definition: (transitive or with a subjunctive clause) To ask for (something).

quote.citation: 1979 December 29, Mitzel, “Dale Barbre's Murder & Related Matters”, in Gay Community News, volume 7, number 23, page 6:
quote.text: Copies of records of Spear's long-distance telephone calls (which had been requested by Norfolk County police from the telephone company)

definitions.definition: Act of requesting (with the adposition at in the presence of possessives, and on in their absence).

quote.citation: c. 1597 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merry Wiues of Windsor”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: I will marry her, sir, at your request.

quote.citation: 1839, The Law Journal for the Year 1832-1949: Comprising Reports:
quote.text: The promise that arises upon an account stated, is to pay on request.

quote.citation: 1690, William Temple, Miscellanea. The Second Part. […], London:  […]  T. M. for Ri[chard] and Ra[lph] Simpson, […], →OCLC, page 49:
quote.text: I do not doubt, but many Great and more Noble Uſes would have been made of ſuch Conqueſts or Diſcoveries, if they had fallen to the ſhare of the Greeks and Romans in thoſe Ages, when Knowledge and Fame were in as great Requeſt, as endleſs Gains and Wealth are among us now; [...]

definitions.definition: (networking) A message sent over a network to a server.
(obsolete) That which is asked for or requested.
